emails.research_note: UK small-business payment culture remains a chronic challenge, with cash-flow pressures and late payments often driven by customer delays and administrative friction. The Government’s 2024 late-payments research found that the most common payment terms are 30 days (54%), but many micro businesses report late payments from customers (32% cite this as a cause of late payments to them) and a notable minority (18%) believe some customers delay payments deliberately as a form of “free finance.” Administrative errors were also a frequent cause (24%), and micro businesses were less likely to pursue late payments formally (about 19%) than larger firms (around 42%), largely to protect relationships. The research also shows that 17% of invoices are late on average across sectors. These findings underpin a staged, relationship-aware chase approach that starts with a gentle nudge and progresses toward firmer action as needed [1]. In addition, independent small-business surveys in 2025 show a sizable share of businesses are owed money (about 62%), with average unpaid invoices around £21,400, and a sizable portion of invoices overdue by 30+ days (about 54%). This evidence reinforces the value of timely reminders and clear payment expectations to protect cash flow in busy hospitality settings [2]. Furthermore, the government’s 2026 Small Business Protections Bill intends to cap large-firm payment terms at 60 days and introduce statutory interest on late payments (8% above the Bank of England base rate), with the Small Business Commissioner empowered to enforce compliance—an important contextual backdrop for practitioners chasing late payments in the UK hospitality sector [3]. The statutory interest framework remains 8% above BoE base rate; current base-rate-linked figures place the rate around 11.75% per year, depending on the BoE base rate at the time [4]. In practice, reputable templates for early-stage Chaser/FreeAgent-style reminders advocate a warm-to-firm progression, and many UK practitioners begin with a non-confrontational reminder before escalating to formal notices if needed [5][6]. References: [1] GOV.UK late payments research: executive summary (Sept 2024) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/late-payments-research-performance-and-practices-across-business/late-payments-research-understanding-variations-in-payment-performance-and-practices-across-business-sizes-html-executive-summary; [2] Intuit QuickBooks UK 2025 Small Business Late Payments Report https://quickbooks.intuit.com/uk/blog/small-business-late-payments-report-2025/; [3] GOV.UK Small Business Protections Bill / 60-day cap and statutory interest https://www.gov.uk/government/news/largest-crackdown-on-late-payments-in-over-25-years-as-landmark-bill-enters-parliament; [4] GOV.UK Charging interest on late commercial payments https://www.gov.uk/late-commercial-payments-interest-debt-recovery/charging-interest-commercial-debt; [5] Chaser: Payment reminder email templates https://www.chaserhq.com/blog/email-templates-friendly-late-payment-reminders-for-your-customers; [6] FreeAgent: Overdue invoice templates https://www.freeagent.com/blog/overdue-invoice-email-templates/;

emails.research_note: A staged approach aligns with observed best practice in UK small-business credit control. GOV.UK’s late-payments research highlights that cash-flow constraints and late payments from customers are common, with administrative errors and deliberate late payments also playing a role; micro businesses are less likely to pursue formal remedies, often to preserve relationships, reinforcing a gentle-to-firm sequencing for chasing payments [1]. The 2025 QuickBooks UK report reinforces the scale of the problem—62% of UK small businesses are owed money, with average unpaid invoices around £21.4k and more than half of invoices overdue by 30+ days—underlining the financial stakes of timely collection and the rationale for a clear but polite escalation when responses stall [2]. The evolving regulatory landscape (60-day cap for large firms and statutory interest on late payments under the Small Business Protections Bill) further supports a firm-but-fair approach and communicates that late payments can carry real costs and consequences, even if the aim remains preserving the business relationship [3]. In terms of practical tools, reputable templates emphasize a progressive escalation (friendly reminder → due-date notice → 1-3 days late gentle reminder → 7 days firm reminder → 14 days payment plan offer) as a standard in the sector [5][6]. References: [1] GOV.UK late payments research: executive summary (Sept 2024) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/late-payments-research-performance-and-practices-across-business-sizes-html-executive-summary; [2] Intuit QuickBooks UK 2025 Small Business Late Payments Report https://quickbooks.intuit.com/uk/blog/small-business-late-payments-report-2025/; [3] GOV.UK Small Business Protections Bill / 60-day cap and statutory interest https://www.gov.uk/government/news/largest-crackdown-on-late-payments-in-over-25-years-as-landmark-bill-enters-parliament; [5] Chaser: Payment reminder email templates https://www.chaserhq.com/blog/email-templates-friendly-late-payment-reminders-for-your-customers; [6] FreeAgent: Overdue invoice templates https://www.freeagent.com/blog/overdue-invoice-email-templates/;

Despite our previous attempts to contact you, payment has not been received for INV-0001 (£1,250.00, now 36 days overdue) or INV-0002 (£875.50, now 21 days overdue). The total overdue balance remains £2,125.50. As outlined in prior correspondence, we are now formally applying our statutory right to charge late-payment interest in accordance with UK law. Please settle the full amount by close of business on [Date: four working days from today] to avoid escalation.

If payment is not received by that deadline, we will proceed with escalation, which may include engaging a debt-recovery agency or referring the matter to the Small Business Commissioner for adjudication. Such actions may incur additional recovery costs, which would be added to your debt. You can settle now via the payment link: [Insert Payment Link]. Please confirm once the transfer has been completed so we can update our accounts.

We value our relationship and sincerely hope to resolve this directly. If you cannot settle in full, contact us promptly to discuss a viable payment plan.

Best regards,
[Your Name]
[Your Cafe Name]
[Phone]
emails.research_note: The final-notice stage commonly triggers formal escalation pathways if payments remain outstanding. GOV.UK guidance confirms statutory interest rights (8% above BoE base rate) and practical steps for debt recovery, while the new Small Business Protections Bill (as of May 2026) introduces a 60-day cap on payment terms for large firms and strengthens enforcement via the Small Business Commissioner; these developments contextualize a clear, time-bound final notice with explicit consequences [4]. Practical templates and policy guidance consistently warn that final notices should be formal and direct, while still leaving room for last-minute settlements or negotiated plans to preserve relationships where possible [5][6][7]. References: [4] GOV.UK charging interest on late commercial payments https://www.gov.uk/late-commercial-payments-interest-debt-recovery/charging-interest-commercial-debt; [4] GOV.UK Largest crackdown on late payments in over 25 years… Small Business Protections Bill https://www.gov.uk/government/news/largest-crackdown-on-late-payments-in-over-25-years-as-landmark-bill-enters-parliament; [5] Chaser: Payment reminder email templates https://www.chaserhq.com/blog/email-templates-friendly-late-payment-reminders-for-your-customers; [6] FreeAgent: Overdue invoice templates https://www.freeagent.com/blog/overdue-invoice-email-templates/; [7] British Business Bank: How to deal with late payments https://www.british-business-bank.co.uk/business-guidance/guidance-articles/finance/how-to-deal-with-late-payments;
